conflara.title: Conflion
conflara.text: Full-function software for running a law firm, built on a conflicts check and new-matter intake. One system on the firm's own server now covers matters and docketing, documents, time and billing, firm accounting links, people and CLE, client relationships, legal holds, the general counsel's office, IT and facilities, and a firm-wide AI layer that suggests while a person decides. Areas of the firm covered 12 Firm roles modelled 7 Passing tests (237 test files) 3,554 Click-through checks in a real browser 360 Synthetic parties benchmarked 3,000,000 Competitors researched 14+ Hit review. Each hit says what it means in plain English, cites the rule, suggests a decision and shows the matters behind it. The AI note is marked as advisory. From a conflicts desk to the whole firm Conflion began as conflicts and intake, and that is still where every matter starts. It now runs the rest of the firm on the same clients, matters and people, with one set of permissions applied on the server and one firm inbox that lists every decision waiting on each person, with a short morning brief for their role. The firm keeps its systems of record (billing, ledger, HR, document and device systems) and Conflion connects them. Matters and docketing A matter workspace with stages, tasks and a record timeline. Court deadlines counted from the rules for California, New York, Texas, Florida, Illinois, Nevada and federal appeals, each step citing its rule, with court notices read into the docket for a clerk to confirm and two-way sync with Outlook or Google calendars. Documents Matter folders made at opening, check-out and check-in with version comments, a profile on every document, email filed to a matter from Outlook, and saved searches for each person. Time, billing and accounting links Time entry with suggested task codes, pre-bills, bill review, invoices, LEDES exports, collections and a pricing desk. Approved journal entries post to the firm's own ledger in QuickBooks Online, Xero or Sage Intacct, with vendor bills, a bank feed, payroll imports, a cash forecast and partner draws. People and CLE One record per person from the HR export, bar admissions and CLE reminders, time away with cover, reviews and feedback, associate development, recruiting, joiners and leavers, and a book test drive for lateral hires before any offer. Client relationships Contacts and every conversation with them, key clients with account plans, feedback at matter close, events, mailing lists with consent, panels and RFPs, referral sources and a client portal. A contact is never mixed into the conflicts records. Risk and the general counsel's office Claims and incidents against the firm, insurance renewals, ownership due diligence on clients, a risk register and a promise ledger. Legal holds with acknowledgements and reminders, and a file destruction review that a hold always stops. The office An IT help desk, a register of the devices and software each person holds, meeting rooms, visitors, post and couriers, and off-site boxes tied to their matters. A leaver's laptop sits on the same checklist as their files and holds. Knowledge and practice support "Who has done this" from the firm's own matters, a clause bank with fallback positions and review dates, precedents, closing sets and signature packets (Conflion never signs), privilege logs and productions, and a staffing board. Ask Newton and the AI tools One question box for the firm whose answers link to the records behind them, and tools that watch the work: matter pulse, an obligation calendar, an early case read, a client risk radar on public sources, bench notes and rule change watch. Each shows its sources, and a person decides. The problem Before a firm takes a matter, it must check every party against everyone it has represented or opposed. Mid-size firms usually search their billing system letter for letter, so they miss parent companies, former names, nicknames and misspellings. Intake is a web form nobody connects to the search, and the enterprise tools are quote-only and installed by consultants. The people involved have different needs. An associate submits the request, a conflicts analyst reviews the hits, practice leaders and general counsel approve, and finance opens the matter. Conflion gives each of seven roles its own view. How the matching works Names are normalized: corporate suffixes stripped, abbreviations expanded, initials collapsed so "A.B.C. Holdings" finds "ABC Holdings". Three scorers combine: a phonetic key (Smith and Smyth), Jaro-Winkler for typos, and trigram overlap for spacing. Rare words weigh more than common ones. People match on surname first, then first name with 30+ nickname pairs (Kate and Katherine), aliases and former names. Strong matches expand two hops through corporate families and one hop through personal links such as spouses and officers. "Kate Okafor" finds the alias "Katherine A. Okafor" and, one hop out, a company where she is an officer that is a current client. Ethical walls: who is screened, who still owes an acknowledgment, and a deny list to export to the document system and time entry. Decisions that come from knowing the work Risk follows the relationship A name match alone means little. Being adverse to a current client on an open matter is high risk; a closed matter is medium; a match only through a personal link is capped below high. Related parties with no matter history are dropped as noise. Rules are built in Former clients point to Rule 1.9, prospective clients to Rule 1.18, lawyer relationships to California Rule 1.7(b) and (c) disclosures. Lateral hires get the 1.10, 1.11 and 1.12 analysis, and engagement letters check the California fee-agreement statutes. Lawyers decide, software suggests The local AI pre-sorts hits and drafts memos, but every AI-filled field carries a mark until a person confirms it. Restricted and walled data never reaches the model, and accepting a suggestion never decides a hit. Least privilege by role Approvers see a summary and a sign-off. Requesters see no firm records while they type. Walls are enforced in what the server sends each user, and every blocked attempt is logged. An audit trail that proves itself The log is append-only with a hash chain and a "Chain intact" check, and database triggers refuse edits. Matters cannot close until the final bill is issued and trust is at zero. Speed for the analyst J and K move between hits, 1 to 5 record a decision, Enter accepts the suggestion, and earlier decisions on the same party appear inline. Under the hood: scale, outside data and a private model Conflion now has about 279,000 lines of TypeScript (about 223,000 of source and 56,000 of tests), 3,554 passing tests across 237 test files, and 360 click-through checks that drive the real app in a browser before each batch of changes is merged. It runs two ways from the same code: a browser-only demo on fictional data, or a firm server with its own database, single sign-on, email and an AI model on the firm's own hardware. Built for a firm with millions of names Row-level storage, incremental sync and server-side search replaced loading everything into the browser. A repeatable benchmark on synthetic firms goes up to 3,000,000 parties, with a written account of what limited a large firm and what changed. Outside entity data, watched nightly A party can be linked to its public-register record: legal-entity data and SEC filings, including subsidiaries read from the latest annual report. A person chooses which names and parents or subsidiaries to add. A nightly job lists what changed for a person to accept or set aside, and cleared requests are flagged for another look. Search that shows its coverage Every search gets a number and shows what it covered. An empty or missing source is never shown as clearance, hits carry plain labels such as "likely same entity" instead of scores, and a no-match result is neutral, not green. Faster hit review A compact hit list with sticky party headers, identity review kept apart from the conflict assessment, and follow-ups tracked until resolved. The suggested order is learned locally from the firm's own past decisions, shows its factors and counts, is off by default, and never hides a hit or records a decision. An offline evaluation of the ranking is written up in the repo. Confidentiality and lateral hires Confidential matters are searched in batch without being revealed: the user is told there is a confidential match and nothing more. Lateral hires get a pre-start checklist with distinct pending, blocked, not-applicable and complete states, each backed by evidence. Compliance records Required documents per request, a summary of each conflict, and tracking for business-associate agreements, joint-representation consents and founder acknowledgements. Measured speed Name search (median): 77 ms to 1.3 ms at 50,000 parties; 535 ms to 5.3 ms at 250,000. Submitting an intake: 1.5 s to 37 ms at 50,000; 8.0 s to 20 ms at 250,000. After a colleague's change, a browser downloads 1 KB instead of reloading 200 KB. Server memory at 250,000 parties: 5.4 GB down to 1.8 GB. All figures come from a benchmark script run on synthetic firms. A model that stays on the firm's hardware The AI runs through Ollama or any OpenAI-compatible local server, so client names never leave the building. It triages hits with a short reason, finds parties in a matter description or pasted email (any name that is not in the text is discarded), drafts a conflicts memo from the recorded decisions only, and suggests column mapping for imports. Every use is written to the audit log with the model name. The ranking model is a separate local statistical fit that uses no AI provider. Teaching and testing inside the app Role-based walkthroughs (open a matter, prepare a request, approve, clear, get your firm live) that point at things but never click, submit or decide. A first-week checklist that ticks itself off from what the person actually does, with tests that limited roles are never shown a step for a page they can't open. A test environment on a fictional firm, marked by a striped banner on every page. It never writes to live data, sends email or calls an outside AI provider. Support without sharing firm data An administrator builds a support bundle of counts, settings switches, versions and error messages with names replaced by placeholders, reads it, then saves it. Nothing is sent automatically, and saving is written to the audit trail. To see a problem happen, support uses a test firm of made-up records at the same size and shape. The live app opens empty, with no sample data, and the desktop app ships for Windows, macOS and Linux with a first-run setup. Market research Comparison with the market. 14+ conflicts and intake products compared with Conflion, feature by feature, from public sources. Newton's full-process pitch: 48 scenes in 14 sections, from the cloud chain a client list travels through in other conflicts products to intake, conflicts, the open matter, its bills and its trust account, all in HTML, CSS and JavaScript with a light and dark mode. How it was built It began as the Conflicts Desk prototype in Claude Code, with tests and CI, and grew into Conflion. I supplied the domain: how conflicts departments actually run, which rules apply, and where existing tools fall short. Claude built the search engine, the synthetic firm and every screen. It then helped compare Conflion with the market from public sources and script and animate the full-process walkthrough. From there I mapped every area of a firm against what Conflion covered and directed the build of each missing one, from docketing and documents to people, client relationships, the general counsel's office and the office itself, with each area's privacy rules set before its screens.

rsc.title: RSC Tool
rsc.text: Two tools for a small remodeling business: an operations app that runs entirely on one Mac, reads the business inbox with a local AI model and never touches the books without the owner's approval, and a phone-first job tracker that shows what each job really earns once crew hours are counted. The problem Jobs, phased payments and expenses lived in a spreadsheet. Receipts, client payments and new leads arrived by email. Estimates, contracts and change orders were written by hand, and nobody could say what a job had cost in labor until it was over. The constraints shaped everything. The owner is not a programmer, client data had to stay on his computer, and nothing could reach the books or a client without his say. The Room Modeler parses feet and inches as typed ("14'6"", "174", "6 1/2"), validates every opening, and draws a dimensioned plan and a 3D view. Sample rooms. Home lists only what needs doing next, across the five groups that replaced 14 tabs. The inbox, read by the local model. Each card says why it matched a job, and nothing is added until the owner presses the green button. What it does Inbox to books Every 30 minutes a local model reads the inbox read-only and returns a fixed JSON shape at temperature 0. Plain code then matches each receipt, payment or lead to a job: a job ID in the email first, then a unique street address, then a unique client surname. If two jobs fit, it asks. Labor cost per job Labor per crew-hour is computed from the estimate's own crew and duration lines, with part-timers counted as half. It warns below the floor rate, compares spend with the estimate's budget, and switches to logged hours once they pass the guess. Money that adds up Job IDs, payment IDs and change-order IDs follow one scheme and double as invoice numbers. Payment schedules are generated by rule and tested to the cent. A change order signed with a finger on a phone updates the contract and schedule together. Hands-free input Any big text box takes speech through a local Whisper model of about 150 MB. Receipt photos and insurance certificates are read by a local vision model, with the job picked by the same rules as email. Runs itself A double-click installer needs no admin password, sizes the models to the Mac's memory, and sets up five background jobs: the app, the mail check, a Monday report, a 6 AM crew sheet and the model server. Daily backups keep 30 copies, and a doctor command checks everything. Built from research A market study of the local remodeling trade set the pricing checks: industry margins imply a 43% materials markup rather than 20%, and the crew-hour floor comes from local wage and billing data. A payment schedule. Each payment ID is also the QuickBooks invoice number, and the page confirms the schedule adds up to the contract. Money owed, grouped by age. Reminders are drafted for the owner to send himself. Every job shows its stage and the one next step, and the Next task button jumps to whatever needs doing. Made-up job from the demo. Since the first version Never lost. A five-stage tracker on every job, a glowing next step, and a Next task button. One-click Send. The estimate goes to the client as a PDF from the owner's own Gmail, only when he presses Send. Every attachment read. Each PDF or photo in an email becomes its own item to review. A downloadable Mac app , built and released automatically when the version changes. In review now: a pricing check before an estimate goes out, a rough range and site-visit questions from a lead's photos, Google review requests, a weekly scorecard of leads and wins, and instant follow-up for website leads. Decisions behind it The model drafts, code decides. Prices, totals, dates, IDs and job matching are computed in code. If a model's draft drops a required fact, the app falls back to a plain template. Fewer fields. A sentence like "Home Depot 109.91 studs for Smith" fills in an expense. Every page keeps a by-hand form for when the model is off. Nothing sent for him. Emails open in his mail app to read and send. Reminders never mention fees or lawyers. Readable by design. The redesign cut 14 tabs to 5 groups, set text at 18px with nothing under 15px, and made every control at least 48px tall. Where it goes next A productizing plan finds about 70% of the app is generic, with the owner-specific parts being configuration rather than architecture. The plan is to treat this business as customer number one, then offer done-for-you setups to three to five local remodelers, with a pilot kit and sales sheet ready. Part two: the crew job tracker The second tool answers one question the owner's spreadsheet could not: after materials, subcontractors and crew time, how much does a job actually leave? Hours were invisible, so every job looked more profitable than it was. The tracker puts crew time on the books as money. Two buttons, every day Today opens with Log hours and Log a cost , because that two-minute habit is what the whole system depends on. Everything else sits below it: what needs a decision, the week's schedule and the job board. Money left, live Set the crew's cost per hour once, and every job shows contract minus materials and subcontractors minus labor. Setup leads with the pricing floor: overhead per hour, break-even and the minimum billable rate. Six screens, built for a phone Today, Jobs, a job (work, money and history tabs), Money across all jobs, Archive and Setup, with a bottom tab bar on phones. The first version had no navigation at all below 680px, so a crew member on a phone could not get around. Change orders and invoices A change order does not move the contract until the customer approves it, and an approved one can be voided, which reverses it out of the total. Invoices flag when they are past due, and a queue lists costs with no receipt. Nothing is ever lost Every removal is reversible and goes to an archive that shows who removed it and why. Deleting a job hides it as a unit and restoring brings back everything attached. Settled records, such as a paid invoice, refuse to delete without an explicit acknowledgement. Built for four people The owner plus up to four crew. The first version had six roles with server-side rules, which was too much for a team that size, so the lightweight version trims permissions to roughly viewer, editor and owner. Two versions, on purpose A full web app. About 6,300 lines across 24 files, with a database, six roles and backups with checksums. Roughly half was inherited from the ChatGPT and Codex first draft; the lifecycle system, query layer, all six screens and the design system are the Claude Code rewrite. It runs on the owner's computer. A shareable version on Claude's artifact pages. Built to be shared with a link. It stores data in the page's shared store and falls back to the phone's own storage if sharing is not available. What testing caught A migration that would have hidden every job. The generated database migration filled a status column with the literal text of its own name, so no job matched "active" and all of them vanished from every screen. It was reproduced against a rebuilt copy of the live database and patched by hand. No mobile viewport tag. The artifact laid out at desktop width and shrank to unreadable on a real phone. It looked fine on a laptop. Two people logging at once. Each person writes only their own document per job, so two crew members cannot overwrite each other. A second phone's entry updated the first live in testing. How it was built Both tools were built with AI. The Mac operations app was built in Claude Code from the owner's real estimates, contract terms and tracker. Claude wrote the code and tests within rules I set. The repo also carries a guide written for the next Claude session on the owner's Mac. It sets out how to explain changes in plain words, back up before any change, keep database migrations additive, test on a copy, and never edit contract text without review.

songs.title: Cat songs and music videos
songs.text: A repeatable way to write songs with Suno, and a toolkit that turns a finished song into a timed storyboard and an animated music video starring my cats. The song workflow The songs are written with Suno, and the process is a written system: concept, style, structure, meter, hook, verses, then a rhyme audit and a length audit before anything is generated. After generating, the song is diagnosed before it is rewritten. The full workflow runs to 17 steps; these are the ideas that matter most. Start with the premise Name the core concept, point of view, emotional tone and the central joke or tension, and brainstorm scenes and images before any lyric. Comedy works best when the singer treats an absurd premise completely seriously. The joke is never explained; it comes out of the character's logic. A separate style prompt Genre, BPM, drum feel, bass, harmony, instruments, vocal register and timbre, texture, space and mood, in under about 1,000 characters. The instrumental should sound like a real record first: future garage, neo-soul, dub, dancehall, vintage calypso, synth-funk, jazz-funk. Funny lyrics don't need funny production, and the contrast is often what makes them funny. Lock structure, then meter Sections are decided before writing, and equivalent sections get equivalent line counts (8, 12 or 16, never a verse that runs long because it has more jokes). A syllable pattern is set per section, such as 8/8/8/8 or 7/10/7/10, with an even stricter meter in the chorus because the music model needs a predictable shape. The hook is designed on its own A short repeated phrase of three to five syllables with a repeated grammatical construction and simple words: "Kitty computer", "No teef, big life". The chorus gets its own identity instead of summarising the verses. Verses are distinct scenes Concrete images, physical detail and character-specific logic. When several characters sing, each has a different worldview, vocabulary and kind of joke, and no two are interchangeable. Rhyme with rules End, internal, multisyllabic and slant rhyme, with several rhyme points inside a line when it comes naturally. No word rhymed with itself, no lazy pseudo-rhymes such as side and outside, and no bent syntax to force a rhyme. Sound beats spelling. Written to be sung Where do the stresses fall, can the singer breathe, are the vowels good for held notes, and does each line have a rhythmic shape like its neighbour? A lyric can look clever on paper and still generate badly if the meter is unstable. Realistic runtime, musical endings The target is about 3:15 to 3:30. If a lyric is too long, cut the weaker jokes and shorten the bridge rather than rush the model. Endings are a refrain, a stripped hook, a harmony stack or an instrumental fade, not a spoken skit. Arrangements that evolve Dropouts, countermelodies, filtered passages, bass breaks, drum changes, vocal stacks, dub-delay throws, sparse bridges and a bigger final chorus, so the track develops instead of looping. Vocals are described precisely, for example a high, clear, intimate lead with airy falsetto edges, close-mic phrasing, whispered doubles and soft stacked harmonies. Quality control before output Fifteen checks run on every lyric: equal line counts in matching verses, the intended syllable pattern, a consistent chorus meter, a short memorable hook, no self-rhymes or lazy rhymes, internal and multisyllabic rhyme present, no line much denser than its neighbours, a lyric that scans out loud, distinct verses, a realistic runtime, a joke that is embodied rather than explained, a musical ending, and a production prompt that sounds like a real record. The output is always two copyable blocks, a style prompt and the lyrics, with no long explanations. Diagnose before rewriting Confused melody: check syllable count and line length. Weak chorus: simplify it and repeat more. Rushed verses: cut density or cut lines. Feels childish: make the production more serious. Forced jokes: go back to character perspective and concrete detail. Weak rhymes: rewrite the rhyme structure instead of patching words. Concept, style, structure, meter, hook, verses, rhyme audit, length audit, generate, diagnose, revise. Cat Music Video Studio A toolkit that connects a recorded song to a timed storyboard and animated character performances. Turning a finished song into a video means coordinating several timelines at once: the recording, the lyrics, the characters' performances and the visual story. Written lyrics don't capture how a singer actually delivers them, and repeated hooks, held vowels, pauses, ad-libs and changed pronunciations all make synchronisation hard. I directed the AI-assisted build of the tool that solves it. An interactive review tool One browser workspace holds the song, the isolated vocal, the lyrics and the storyboard. Words and lines are clickable to audition them, master and vocal switch without losing your place, and playback speed slows difficult phrases. A waveform seeks on click, the current word highlights live, and search and section filters move through verses and choruses. Review flags and confidence labels mark uncertain alignment, and a storyboard view ties timed scenes to actions, camera direction, continuity notes and generation prompts. Audio analysis and alignment Scripts decode the master and the isolated vocal, measure both, and compare sync at several points. Whisper recognition and reference-conditioned alignment propose word and line timings, and separate analysis of each stem gives evidence to compare them. Targeted passes handle the hard parts: repeated calls, short interjections and closing phrases. The data keeps supplied lyrics, model recognition, candidate timestamps and unresolved events apart, so uncertainty stays visible. Production data other tools can use JSON for timing maps, audio metadata, lyrics, scenes and review evidence. CSV for word and line timings, sections, non-lyric intervals, scene plans and review logs. SRT for draft captions. HTML for an interactive review package with the timing data embedded. Together they give audio, shots, captions and animation one shared timeline. The songs Fourteen songs so far, all starring my cats, written and generated with the workflow above and collected in one YouTube playlist . Why You Chase Me, Newty? On Mi Turf No Teef, Big Life Mommy Saved Mi Who Puke Pon di Floor? Vet Day Come Mi Nah Like Moving Day Every Lane, Every Road Free Di Claw Shoulda Leave di Treats Alone Please Turn on di Sink Flea Pon Me Kitty Computer Open up the Door A finished animation A complete music video built in the browser with p5.js, combining character drawings, environments, timed shots, captions and the original song. Mouth opening follows word timing and vocal amplitude, the mouth closes between timed words, and singing can be switched on or off per shot. Mouth and tongue shapes respond to the resulting value. It has play, seek, restart, mute, caption and fullscreen controls, plus a rendered vertical-video version. "Every Lane, Every Road": a 34-shot animated video, about 3 minutes 33 seconds, exported at 1080 × 1920 and 25 fps. "Why You Run Me Down, Newty?": 627 word records and 44 proposed shots. "Mommy Save Mi": 567 word records and 42 proposed shots. Built with Python, Whisper small.en, stable-ts, FFmpeg, NumPy, SciPy, soundfile, JavaScript, HTML and CSS, and p5.js. My role I set the creative goals, supplied the songs and characters, directed the AI-assisted build, and shaped the workflow through requirements and feedback. It was built through an iterative ChatGPT and Codex workflow, which wrote the implementation, analysis scripts, production documents and animation code.

specimenroom.title: Specimen Room
specimenroom.text: A live design reference archive of 1,520 working specimens in 31 cabinets, from palettes, type and shaders to scroll effects, ornament and ASCII art, plus a website builder that assembles a whole one-page site from them. Every specimen can be tuned on the spot and copied as standalone code. Live specimens 1,520 Cabinets 31 Specimens with live controls 1,322 Gradients and shaders 133 ASCII and glyph pieces 150 Site themes in the builder 14 The front of the archive. The rail lists every cabinet, and a random specimen sits on the bench, running live. How it grew The archive went from 825 specimens to 1,520 in three days, in batches. Each batch was rendered, screenshotted wing by wing and checked before it went in, and every specimen keeps a permanent accession number, so nothing already cited moves. Oct 26 825 Oct 26 947 Oct 27 1,080 Oct 27 1,211 Oct 28 1,248 Oct 28 1,520 The later batches came from three places: ideas rebuilt from scratch, ports from openly licensed libraries (shadcn, daisyUI, Tremor, Magic UI, Paper Shaders and others) with each license kept on the specimen, and a batch of form and section specimens written by Gemini from a house guide and held to the same checks. What each specimen gives you A live sample, drawn in the browser rather than shown as a picture. Controls built from the specimen's own settings, so a palette, a seed or a speed can be changed and seen at once. Standalone code that reproduces exactly what is on screen, with a copy button. A permanent accession number, its source and its license, so a specimen can be cited in a brief. How a page with 1,520 live pieces stays fast Loaded by cabinet: each cabinet's code arrives only when one of its specimens is about to be seen. Mounted near the screen only, a few per frame, and stopped again when scrolled away. Animation also pauses in background tabs. A WebGL budget: browsers keep about 16 live 3D contexts, so the archive holds at most 9 and unloads the ones farthest from the middle of the screen. Sealed styles: every specimen renders in its own shadow root, so no specimen's CSS can leak into another. A specimen sheet: the live piece, its controls, the code and where the idea came from. Where this site's effects came from The picture index, the numbers that count up, the paper grain, the shader backdrops, the before-and-after sliders and the reading bar on this page were all chosen from the archive and rebuilt to fit this site's colours and appearance settings. Specimen Builder: a website from the archive Describe a business in a sentence, such as a record shop with a listening bar, and the builder lays out a one-page site from the archive's navigation bars, heroes, sections, forms and footers. Then it makes the result look like one site instead of a collage of seven. Library, page and suggestions. The panel on the right only offers blocks that fit the slot after the selected one. What makes it helpful Starts from a brief. Claude picks a starter page of five to eight blocks and says why each fits. Without Claude, a local scorer fills the same slots from the brief's words, so it always works. One theme for the whole site. Fourteen themes built from the archive's own palettes and type pairings, or "from this block" to borrow the look of one you like. Copy for your business. Claude rewrites each block's text for the brief, keeping lengths close, and every line can be edited by hand. Exports one file that rebuilds the page on load, as a normal web page or a page ready to publish on Claude. The hard part: one site, not a collage Every specimen arrives with its own fonts, colours and invented brand. The re-skin pass reads every colour in a block, sorts it by tone against that block's own background, and maps it onto the theme's ramp, with strong colours becoming the accent. Fonts follow the theme, and the shop's name replaces each specimen's fake brand in headers and footers. A final pass pushes any text below the AA contrast standard back toward legibility. Checked on 231 blocks across seven cabinets with no render errors, and on 156 text pairs in three themes with none below AA. The same check on the unthemed page finds failures, so it can fail. Fourteen site themes, each a palette and a type pairing from the archive. An exported page in one theme. Seven blocks from seven different specimens, one palette and one set of fonts. How it was built Built with Claude Code under my direction. I chose what goes into each cabinet and judged every specimen; Claude wrote the specimens, the catalog, the archive's viewer and the Specimen Builder, and Gemini added two batches of form and section specimens following a written guide. When the first version of the builder produced collages, I said so, and the second version was rebuilt around the theme and re-skin pass.

blackbox.title: BLACKBOX
blackbox.text: A flight recorder for AI coding agents. It captures what Claude Code actually did, prompts, tool calls, file edits, failures and subagent handoffs, and lets you replay a session, trace a file change back to the agent that made it, and see how a failure was recovered. Nothing leaves the Mac. The flight recorder. Every track of a session on one timeline, played back at up to 20x, with the inspector showing what led to a failed test and what came next. The problem AI coding agents now run for long stretches, start subagents and edit dozens of files. When something breaks, the only record is a scrolling transcript. There is no way to see the session as a whole, ask which agent changed a file, or tell what was observed from what someone guessed afterward. What it does Capture, local only: opt-in hooks and transcript import into a local database, with privacy levels and redaction. Replay on a single timeline, with an inspector that links each event to its cause and result. File forensics, agent topology and a failure observatory that groups repeated failures and reconstructs recovery. A safe installer that shows a line-by-line diff of the Claude settings file and backs it up before changing anything. The failure observatory. Observed events and inferred steps are marked differently, and your own hypotheses are kept apart from both. The same recorder in a white skin. Nine skins are available, chosen in Settings rather than in the working screens. How it was built A native macOS app in SwiftUI over SQLite with full-text search. I wrote the specification package and asked for it to be as sleek as a flight instrument; Claude Code built the app, the hook relay and the synthetic sessions, and ran the builds on my Mac through Remote Control.

byzantium.title: Byzantium
byzantium.text: An illustrated encyclopedia of the Eastern Roman Empire, 324 to 1453, built around a mosaic atlas you can drag through 1,129 years and watch the borders move. Dated territory snapshots 200 Map features 11,850 Encyclopedia entries 464 Licensed images 1,174 Podcast episodes indexed 440 Invalid geometries / overlaps 0 / 0 The atlas at 1025, near the empire's height. Every tile is a tessera; the panel says who was on the throne and who held what that year. The atlas Drawn as a mosaic Territory is one fixed grid of tesserae, each slightly varied in shade, with grout between them. The empire is imperial purple edged in gold; the sea is blue tile. A Borders mode switches to clean outlines, and light and dark themes each have their own palette. Conquest you can watch When borders change, only the tiles that changed owner turn over, in a wave that starts from the conqueror's side, so territory is taken rather than repainted. Cities that change hands send out a ripple. Built for scrubbing Drag, click or use the keyboard; play at 1 to 50 years a second; or press Next change to jump to the next year the map moves.
